name: Judy Garland
milestone_by_age_26: Starred as Dorothy in The Wizard of Oz (1939) at age 17, winning a special Academy Juvenile Award, and had become an MGM star with multiple hit films by her mid-twenties.
early_history_summary: Garland began performing at age two with her sisters in her father's movie theater in Grand Rapids, Minnesota. She signed a seven-year contract with MGM in September 1935 at age 13 and achieved international fame with The Wizard of Oz in 1939.
family_context_summary: Born to vaudevillian parents who operated a movie theater in Grand Rapids, Minnesota; mother accompanied the Gumm Sisters on piano.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were former vaudevillians; father Francis Avent Gumm operated the New Grand Theatre where Judy first performed at age two.
primary_early_advantage_tags: vaudeville family, theater ownership, early stage exposure, MGM contract, prodigy vocalist
evidence_summary: Garland's early career was propelled by deep family-domain immersion — both parents were vaudevillians and her father owned the theater where she first performed at age two. Her extraordinary vocal ability was recognized immediately, leading to an MGM contract at 13 without a screen test. The MGM studio system provided the elite institutional pipeline and distribution that made her a star by 17 with The Wizard of Oz. Her father's death when she was 13 and family financial pressures created adversity but also urgency.

name: David Woodard

early_history_summary: Woodard studied at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music and moved to Napa, California in 1987 where he worked at Tulocay Cemetery. His notable creative outputs began in the 1990s.
evidence_summary: No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found. Woodard's notable creative work began in the 1990s, well after age 26.

name: Peter Gabriel
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Genesis at Charterhouse School in 1967 (age 17), released debut album From Genesis to Revelation in 1969 (age 19), and by age 26 had released multiple progressive rock classics including Nursery Cryme (1971), Foxtrot (1972), and Selling England by the Pound (1973).
early_history_summary: Gabriel formed Garden Wall with schoolmate Tony Banks at Charterhouse School in 1965, which merged into Genesis in 1967. Their debut album was released in 1969, and Gabriel became known for his theatrical stage performances as Genesis's lead vocalist and principal lyricist.
family_context_summary: Born to Ralph Parton Gabriel, an electrical engineer and dairy farm owner, and Edith Irene, from a musical family. His great-great-great-uncle was Lord Mayor of London. Raised at Deep Pool Farm, a Victorian manor near Chobham.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an electrical engineer and dairy farm owner from a family of London timber importers; mother came from a musical family and gave him piano lessons. No direct music industry connection.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Charterhouse School, peer band formation, progressive rock wave, public school education, Tony Banks collaboration
evidence_summary: Gabriel's early career was catalyzed by the peer network at Charterhouse School, where he met Tony Banks, Mike Rutherford, and Anthony Phillips. Together they formed Genesis in 1967 and released their debut album in 1969. His family provided a comfortable upbringing at a Victorian manor and public school education but had no direct music industry connections. The progressive rock wave of the early 1970s provided a structural tailwind for the band's artistic direction.

name: Vladimir Ashkenazy
milestone_by_age_26: Won second prize at the V International Chopin Piano Competition in Warsaw in 1955 (age 18) and first prize at the Queen Elisabeth Music Competition in Brussels in 1956 (age 19), establishing international prominence as a concert pianist.
early_history_summary: Ashkenazy began playing piano at age six and was accepted to the Central Music School at age eight. He studied at the Moscow Conservatory under Lev Oborin and Boris Zemliansky, winning major international piano competitions by age 19.
family_context_summary: Born to pianist and composer David Ashkenazi and actress Yevstolia Grigorievna in Gorky, Soviet Union. Father was Jewish and mother came from a Russian Orthodox family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father David Ashkenazi was a professional pianist and composer; mother was an actress. The family provided direct musical domain immersion from birth.
primary_early_advantage_tags: pianist father, Central Music School, Moscow Conservatory, early competition success, Lev Oborin mentorship
evidence_summary: Ashkenazy's early success was built on deep family-domain immersion — his father was a professional pianist and composer — and access to the elite Soviet music education pipeline, starting at the Central Music School at age eight and the Moscow Conservatory. Sustained mentorship from Anaida Sumbatyan and then Lev Oborin, combined with intensive practice from age six, led to major international competition prizes by ages 18-19. KGB harassment as a student added adversity.

name: Theo Angelopoulos
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Angelopoulos studied law and film at IDHEC in Paris, then worked as a journalist and film critic. He made his first short film in 1968 (age 33) and his first feature in 1972 (age 37). His Palme d'Or came in 1998.
early_history_summary: Angelopoulos studied law at the University of Athens, then attended IDHEC in Paris before returning to Greece as a journalist and film critic. He began making films after the 1967 Greek military coup.
family_context_summary: Born in Athens; father Spyros hailed from Ampeliona in the Peloponnese. Father was taken hostage during the Greek Civil War when Angelopoulos was 9.
evidence_summary: No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found. Angelopoulos was still a student and journalist in his twenties; his filmmaking career began at age 33.

name: Tina Turner
milestone_by_age_26: Released 'A Fool in Love' in July 1960 (age 20), which reached #2 on the R&B chart and #27 on the Billboard Hot 100, establishing her as Tina Turner and launching the Ike and Tina Turner Revue.
early_history_summary: Turner began singing in her church choir in Nutbush, Tennessee. She met Ike Turner and his Kings of Rhythm at Club Manhattan in East St. Louis around 1956-1957, began performing with the band, and made her recording debut as 'Little Ann' in 1958. Her breakout came with 'A Fool in Love' in 1960.
family_context_summary: Born Anna Mae Bullock in Brownsville, Tennessee to sharecropper parents. Father worked as overseer of sharecroppers at Poindexter Farm. Mother left the family when Turner was 11. Family lived in poverty in rural Tennessee.
parent_family_domain_summary: No documented family domain advantage in music; first cousin once removed was bluesman Eugene Bridges.
primary_early_advantage_tags: poverty, sharecropper background, church choir, Ike Turner mentorship, St. Louis club scene, R&B wave
evidence_summary: Turner's early career emerged from extreme adversity — poverty, abandonment by her mother, and racial segregation in rural Tennessee. Her powerful vocal talent was recognized by Ike Turner when she was 17, leading to mentorship and eventual breakout with 'A Fool in Love' at age 20. The St. Louis and East St. Louis club scene and the Chitlin' Circuit provided the performance infrastructure for her early success. No family financial platform or domain advantage was documented.

name: Donald Sutherland
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Sutherland was performing in repertory theatre in Scotland from 1960 (age 25) and had small British film and TV roles in the early 1960s, but his breakthrough came with The Dirty Dozen in 1967 (age 32).
early_history_summary: Sutherland graduated from the University of Toronto in 1958, studied at LAMDA, and acted at the Perth Repertory Theatre from 1960. He gained small roles in British horror films and TV through the mid-1960s before his breakthrough in The Dirty Dozen (1967).
family_context_summary: Born in Saint John, New Brunswick, Canada. Father Frederick McLea Sutherland worked in sales and ran the local gas, electricity, and bus company. Suffered rheumatic fever, hepatitis, and polio as a child.
evidence_summary: No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found. Sutherland was doing repertory theatre and minor film/TV roles in his mid-twenties; his breakthrough came at age 32 with The Dirty Dozen (1967).

name: Tsung-Dao Lee
milestone_by_age_26: Completed PhD under Enrico Fermi at the University of Chicago in 1950 (age 23), conducted postdoctoral research at UC Berkeley and the Institute for Advanced Study Princeton, and joined Columbia University as assistant professor in 1953 (age 26), where he developed the Lee Model in quantum field theory.
early_history_summary: Lee showed early aptitude for physics in China, studying at National Chekiang University and National Southwestern Associated University before receiving a Chinese government fellowship to study at the University of Chicago in 1946. He completed his PhD under Enrico Fermi in 1950 and joined Columbia as assistant professor at age 26.
family_context_summary: Born in Shanghai to Chun-kang Lee, a chemical industrialist and merchant involved in China's early fertilizer development, and a mother who moved to Taiwan in the 1950s. Father was one of the first graduates of the University of Nanking.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a chemical industrialist and merchant with university education; no direct physics domain transfer documented, but family valued education sufficiently to support advanced study.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Fermi mentorship, University of Chicago, IAS Princeton, Columbia, Chinese government fellowship, WWII education disruption
evidence_summary: Lee's early career was propelled by exceptional intellectual ability recognized by senior physicists, leading to mentorship under Enrico Fermi at the University of Chicago (PhD at 23) and postdoctoral work at UC Berkeley and IAS Princeton under Oppenheimer's endorsement. He joined Columbia as assistant professor at 26, where his Lee Model work began. His father's industrial background provided educational support, but the key accelerants were the elite institutional pipeline and Fermi's mentorship. WWII's disruption of his Chinese education created urgency without blocking his trajectory.

name: Ian McKellen
milestone_by_age_26: Made his West End debut in 'A Scent of Flowers' at the Duke of York's theatre in 1964 (age 25), winning the Clarence Derwent Award for best supporting actor, and joined Laurence Olivier's National Theatre Company at the Old Vic in 1965 (age 25-26).
early_history_summary: McKellen developed an interest in theatre from childhood, influenced by his parents' amateur dramatics. He won a scholarship to Cambridge University in 1958 where he joined the Marlowe Society and appeared in 23 plays. After graduating, he spent four years in regional repertory theatre before his West End breakthrough in 1964.
family_context_summary: Born in Burnley, Lancashire to Margery Lois and Denis Murray McKellen. Father was promoted and the family relocated to Bolton in 1951. Family was involved in amateur dramatics.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were involved in amateur dramatics; sister Jean acted, directed, and produced amateur theatre. No professional theatre domain transfer documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Cambridge Marlowe Society, repertory theatre, National Theatre Company, Olivier, early stage reps
evidence_summary: McKellen's early career was built on massive early reps — 23 plays in 3 years at Cambridge's Marlowe Society followed by 4 years in regional repertory theatre. The Cambridge theatre ecosystem connected him with directors like Peter Hall and peers like Derek Jacobi. His family's amateur dramatics sparked early interest but provided no professional network. The cumulative practice and institutional pipeline led to his West End debut and Clarence Derwent Award at 25, followed by selection for Olivier's National Theatre Company.

name: Maya Plisetskaya
milestone_by_age_26: Graduated from the Bolshoi Ballet School in 1943 (age 18) and joined the Bolshoi Ballet company, quickly rising to become their leading soloist, performing major roles including The Dying Swan and Odette-Odile in Swan Lake by her early twenties.
early_history_summary: Plisetskaya studied ballet at the Bolshoi Ballet School from age nine under Elizaveta Gerdt and her aunt Sulamith Messerer. She first performed at the Bolshoi Theatre at age 11. Despite family tragedy — her father was executed in Stalin's purges and her mother imprisoned — she graduated and joined the Bolshoi Ballet in 1943.
family_context_summary: Born into a prominent Lithuanian Jewish family involved in theater and film. Mother Rachel Messerer was a silent-film actress. Uncle Asaf Messerer was Bolshoi Ballet principal dancer; aunt Sulamith Messerer was Bolshoi prima ballerina. Father Mikhail Plisetski was a diplomat and engineer who was executed during Stalin's purges.
parent_family_domain_summary: Extensive family involvement in ballet and theater: maternal aunt Sulamith Messerer was a Bolshoi prima ballerina who adopted and trained Maya; uncle Asaf Messerer was a Bolshoi principal dancer; mother was a silent-film actress.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Bolshoi Ballet family, Sulamith Messerer training, Bolshoi School, Stalinist persecution, wartime ballet, early Bolshoi debut
evidence_summary: Plisetskaya's early career was profoundly shaped by her family's deep immersion in ballet and theater — her aunt Sulamith Messerer was a Bolshoi prima ballerina who adopted and trained her, and her uncle Asaf Messerer was a Bolshoi principal dancer. This family-domain apprenticeship, combined with elite institutional training at the Bolshoi School, led to her joining the Bolshoi Ballet as a soloist at 18. Extreme adversity from Stalinist persecution (father executed, mother imprisoned) created both urgency and a refuge in ballet.

name: Brian Wilson
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded the Beach Boys in 1961 (age 19), released debut single 'Surfin'' and signed with Capitol Records in 1962 (age 20), and by age 26 had written or co-written more than two dozen Top 40 hits including 'I Get Around' (1964), 'Help Me, Rhonda' (1965), and 'Good Vibrations' (1966), as well as producing the landmark album Pet Sounds (1966).
early_history_summary: Wilson showed musical aptitude from early childhood, learning melodies by ear as an infant. His father Murry Wilson cultivated the children's musical talents but was also violent and cruel. Brian began four-part harmonies with a tape recorder at age 16 and co-founded the Beach Boys in 1961 with his brothers Dennis and Carl, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine.
family_context_summary: Born in Inglewood, California to Murry Wilson, a machinist who later pursued songwriting part-time, and Audree Neva. Father was violent and cruel. Family was working-class, living in Hawthorne, California.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Murry Wilson was a machinist who pursued songwriting part-time and actively cultivated the children's musical talents, though he was also physically and psychologically abusive. Father acted as the Beach Boys' first manager.
primary_early_advantage_tags: family band, Beach Boys formation, Southern California surf culture, Capitol Records, father songwriter, abusive childhood
evidence_summary: Wilson's early career was built on his extraordinary musical intuition — learning melodies by ear as an infant and creating four-part harmonies by age 16. The Beach Boys were a family-band formation with his brothers and cousin, amplified by the Southern California surf culture wave. His father Murry's songwriting aspirations and music publishing connections helped launch the band, though his abuse was a significant adversity. Wilson's pioneering production skills and songwriting led to multiple Top 40 hits and Pet Sounds by age 24.

name: Makoto Kobayashi
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Kobayashi graduated from Nagoya University in 1967 (age 23) and was still a graduate student at age 26. His DSc was completed in 1972 (age 28) and his landmark CP-violation work with Toshihide Maskawa was published in 1973 (age 29).
early_history_summary: Kobayashi graduated from the School of Science of Nagoya University in 1967 and pursued doctoral research under Shoichi Sakata. His DSc was completed in 1972, after which he became a research associate at Kyoto University and began his landmark work with Maskawa on CP violation.
family_context_summary: Born in Nagoya, Japan in 1944. Father Hisashi died when Kobayashi was two. Family home was destroyed in the bombing of Nagoya. Cousin Toshiki Kaifu became Prime Minister of Japan; another cousin Norio Kaifu was an astronomer.
evidence_summary: No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found. Kobayashi was a graduate student at Nagoya University through his mid-twenties; his doctoral degree and landmark CP-violation research came at ages 28-29.
